blocks.content: FEDERAL SYSTEM OF INDIA

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Article 1 of the Constitution describes India as a 'Union of States' rather than a 'Federation of States'.
The Seventh Schedule classifies legislative subjects into three distinct lists: Union List, State List, and Concurrent List.
Residuary powers of legislation are vested exclusively in the Centre/Parliament under Article 248.
The Indian constitutional setup is characterized as 'Quasi-Federal' with a strong unitary bias during emergencies.
Cooperative and Competitive federalism drive modern inter-state and financial relations in India.

blocks.content: The Federal System of India refers to the division of powers between the Central Government and the State Governments.
It ensures that power is not concentrated in one authority and that governance is carried out at different levels.
India follows a unique model of federalism which is often described as:
The federal structure of India is enshrined in the Constitution and is considered part of its Basic Structure.
MEANING OF FEDERALISM
Federalism is a system of government in which:

items:
• Powers are divided between two or more levels of government
  • Each level functions independently within its jurisdiction
  • The Constitution is supreme
  • Judiciary acts as the interpreter of the Constitution
Powers are divided between two or more levels of government
Each level functions independently within its jurisdiction
Judiciary acts as the interpreter of the Constitution

blocks.content: In a federal system, neither the Centre nor the States are subordinate to each other in their respective spheres.
EVOLUTION OF FEDERALISM IN INDIA
The idea of federalism in India developed gradually during British rule. Important milestones:

items:
• Government of India Act, 1935 – Introduced federal features
  • Indian Independence Act, 1947 – Gave autonomy to provinces
  • Constitution of India, 1950 – Established a federal system with strong centre
Government of India Act, 1935 – Introduced federal features
Indian Independence Act, 1947 – Gave autonomy to provinces
Constitution of India, 1950 – Established a federal system with strong centre

blocks.content: The framers adopted federalism to manage India’s diversity and vast geographical size.
NATURE OF INDIAN FEDERALISM
The Indian Constitution does not explicitly use the word 'federal'. However, India is considered a federal state because:

items:
• Dual government exists
  • Written Constitution
  • Division of powers
  • Supremacy of Constitution
  • Independent judiciary

blocks.content: At the same time, India has a strong central government, making it a quasi-federal system.
FEATURES OF FEDERAL SYSTEM IN INDIA
Major features include:
DIVISION OF POWERS (SEVENTH SCHEDULE)
The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution divides powers between Centre and States into three lists:

items: Union List – Subjects of national importance
State List – Subjects of state importance
Concurrent List – Subjects of common interest

blocks.content: In case of conflict, Union Law prevails over State Law.

Emergency Provisions (Articles 352, 356, and 360) convert the federal structure into a unitary one without formal constitutional amendment.

blocks.content: CONCLUSION
The federal system of India is unique in nature.
It combines the features of both federal and unitary systems.
While the Centre is strong, the States play a vital role in governance.
This balance ensures unity, integrity, and efficient administration of the country.
